analysis.one_liner: ONGC is India's largest crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, a Government of India-controlled PSU that also holds large stakes in refiners MRPL and HPCL.
analysis.whats_happening: ONGC's board has declared a record interim dividend of Rs 8/share, with the record date falling on 12 November 2026 - just days away and the highest-ever single interim payout for the company. This follows Q2 FY27 results (reported 5 November 2026): consolidated PAT rose 46.9% YoY to roughly Rs 18,535 crore, and H1 FY27 standalone PAT hit a record Rs 32,522 crore (+82% YoY), driven almost entirely by a sharp jump in crude oil price realisation tied to the Middle East conflict-driven price spike earlier in 2026, even as ONGC's own crude and gas output fell.
analysis.plain_terms: ONGC pumps crude oil and natural gas out of the ground and sells it, so its profit moves with global oil prices far more than with anything the company itself does. This quarter's big profit jump looks impressive, but almost none of it came from producing more oil - production actually fell. It came from oil fetching a much higher price than a year ago, for reasons unrelated to ONGC (a geopolitical conflict). That is a less durable kind of profit growth, and it can fade just as fast as it appeared if oil prices cool.
analysis.quarters: Standalone revenue was Rs 43,875 crore (+32.8% YoY, -5.6% QoQ) with standalone PAT of Rs 15,489 crore (+57.3% YoY, -9.1% QoQ); consolidated PAT was about Rs 18,535 crore (+46.9% YoY). The driver was crude realisation of $92.33/bbl versus $67.34/bbl a year earlier (+37%), while actual output fell - crude to 4.437 MMT from 4.630 MMT, gas to 4.839 BCM from 4.918 BCM. On the 6 November earnings call, management guided to roughly 29 MMTOE of output for FY27 and flagged that the flagship KG-DWN-98/2 deepwater project is producing only 19,000-28,000 bpd versus an original target of 45,000 bpd, citing reservoir complexity worse than expected. Capex guidance for FY27 was inconsistent across disclosures (figures cited ranged from roughly Rs 30,000-33,000 crore to $3.5-4 billion) - treat the exact number as unconfirmed.
analysis.performance_read: The stock closed at Rs 234.8, down 23.4% from its August 2024 peak of Rs 306.57, though still mid-range within its 52-week band of Rs 219.8-300.12. This fall is not a corporate-action artifact - ONGC's three splits (2006, 2011, 2016) are already reflected in the price series and there has been no demerger - so the drawdown is a genuine price decline. Over 5 years the stock has returned 104.78% versus Nifty's 38.29% and peer Reliance's 16.84%, largely riding the 2022-2024 oil price cycle and its dividend. But the 1-year return is roughly flat at -1.65% (Nifty -2.3%, Reliance -10.69%), underlining that this is a cyclical, oil-price-linked stock rather than a steady compounder.
analysis.valuation_read: At roughly 5.9x earnings and 0.74x book, with a 5.64% trailing dividend yield (set to rise further once the 12 November interim dividend is included), ONGC looks statistically cheap on conventional metrics. Why it is cheap: it is a state-owned commodity producer whose current earnings are inflated by an oil-price spike that is unlikely to be the new normal, and its production base is shrinking (-3% YoY), so today's margins overstate steady-state earning power. Whether it is actually cheap depends on what crude price you assume for the next few years - at a lower through-cycle oil price, the effective multiple on normalised earnings would be higher than 5.9x suggests.
analysis.growth_read: This is clearly price-led, not volume-led growth - the textbook pattern that is less durable in a commodity business. Both crude and gas output fell about 3% YoY even as revenue and profit jumped on a 37% rise in crude realisation. The one project meant to add real volume, KG-DWN-98/2, is running at 19,000-28,000 bpd versus a planned 45,000 bpd, so the company's main volume-growth lever is currently underdelivering.
analysis.health_read: ROCE of 14.2% and ROE of 11.6% are respectable, and debt-to-equity of roughly 0.47 (debt ~Rs 1,74,316 crore against equity ~Rs 3,71,958 crore) is not alarming for a capital-intensive E&P business. Whether PAT is converting cleanly into operating cash flow could not be verified - check on Screener. The bigger concern here is business risk, not financial risk: a shrinking domestic production base, execution shortfalls at KG-98/2, and capital tied up overseas - subsidiary ONGC Videsh has over $500 million in stuck Venezuela dividend receivables and just received a fresh Rs 10,000 crore loan facility from the parent.
analysis.ownership_read: The promoter, the Government of India, holds 58.89% with 0% pledge, as expected for a PSU. FIIs hold about 8.55-8.56% and DIIs about 18.66%, with LIC as the largest single institutional holder at roughly 10.3%. There is no marquee individual investor on the register - plainly, none was found. Note that the 58.89% promoter figure appears identically across several recent quarters in secondary sources, which may indicate stale aggregator data rather than confirmed current holding - worth a direct check on Screener.
strengths: TTM dividend yield of 5.64% (Rs 13.25/share), with a record Rs 8/share interim dividend just declared (record date 12 November 2026) - among the highest cash yields in the large-cap space.
Consolidated PAT up 46.9% YoY to about Rs 18,535 crore in Q2 FY27, with H1 FY27 standalone PAT a record Rs 32,522 crore (+82% YoY).
Valuation re-rating room: P/E of roughly 5.9x and P/B of 0.74x, both well below the broader market.
Zero promoter pledge and government backing, which reduces governance and default tail-risk relative to private commodity producers.
watchpoints: Crude and gas output fell about 3% YoY (crude 4.437 MMT vs 4.630 MMT; gas 4.839 BCM vs 4.918 BCM) - the profit surge is price-driven, not volume-driven, and could reverse if crude realisation cools from the current elevated level.
The flagship KG-DWN-98/2 deepwater project is producing only 19,000-28,000 bpd against an original 45,000 bpd target, due to reservoir complexity - the key growth project is underdelivering.
Capex guidance for FY27 is inconsistent across company disclosures (figures ranging from about Rs 30,000-33,000 crore to $3.5-4 billion) - lack of clarity on committed spend.

Overseas subsidiary ONGC Videsh has over $500 million in stuck Venezuela dividend receivables and just drew a fresh Rs 10,000 crore loan facility from ONGC - capital allocation and geopolitical risk worth monitoring.
analysis.one_thing: Watch the crude oil price realisation in Q3 FY27 (results expected late January-mid February 2027): since ONGC's own production is shrinking, a cooling of the Indian crude basket from its current elevated range would directly reverse the profit growth seen this quarter.
analysis.data_notes: Q2 FY27 standalone and consolidated figures were cross-checked across the NSE filing, Business Standard, PSU Watch, Rigzone, Taxguru and PSU Connect, and were consistent; one outlier consolidated PAT figure (Rs 16,744 crore, from a single secondary outlet) was set aside. Valuation ratios are from Screener.in, cross-checked against Trendlyne (P/E 5.89, consistent); one outlier P/E of 6.93 from a different source was set aside as likely a different earnings basis. Not verified: operating cash flow versus PAT conversion, the exact FY27 capex figure (three different numbers appear across sources), and whether the 58.89% promoter holding is current or a repeated stale figure - check directly on Screener.
